Okay... but in this context, if you're trying to do gene modifications on human embryos to make them resistant to HIV, you either need (1) a gamete donor with HIV, or (2) infect the resulting child of said modifications with HIV at some point, to test.

I'd assume that you'd want to go with the former, if only because it might be possible to detect if the embryo has been infected with HIV before it qualifies as people, so the pregnancy could be terminated if it wound up with HIV. The combination of the nature of the disease and the technologies we're developing makes the blanket rule a bit absurd, because honestly, how else are you going to test this shit without getting into even worse moral grey areas?

Much of the commentary on this incident revolves around the ethics of the experiment, but there are other more technical issues that remain to be addressed. Here is a run down on some of them. To my mind they revolve around two major issues, and the problem is complicated by the fact that the researcher's announcement by press release is lacking in what could allow a proper evaluation of his work and potential replication.

The first question - Did it work ?

The short answer is no. Leaving aside the 30 some embryos discarded for unstated reasons the researcher himself admitted that only one of the two girls is homozygous for the edited gene. The other is heterozygous and therefore continues to be susceptible to HIV. Then there is the probability that what he has produced are 'genetic mosaics'. This means that the supposedly successful modifications are present only in some of the cells in the infants' bodies but not in others. Hence those cells, and the bodies that carry them are still susceptible to HIV. I repeat, this is not a "possibility" but rather a probability.

The second question - what are the potential risks of this sort of procedure ?

This presently unknown, but the evidence points to the fact that there are indeed risks even in the simple case that only the gene in question was modified. This is compounded by the fact that CRISPR technology is a work in progress, and the occurrence of what are called 'off-target' changes to the genome has yet to be solved. This is less of a problem with simple gene deletion, but it is major in gene modification. The evidence presented so far is that the researcher has basically not addressed this problem at all.

For both questions any firm answers are far in the future assuming that the work is neither fraudulent nor incompetent. The latter two descriptions are actually very likely from what is known now.
